blocks.text: Regulations for the Twelve-Hour Buddha-Recitation at Yongquan and Huxin Monasteries

inline.s: The Buddha taught that the birth and death of sentient beings is measured in long ages, piling up days and nights until they run through kalpas unending, never resting, never ceasing. It comes from thought after thought of deluded clinging; never is there a single thought that pauses even for a moment. Because delusion never breaks off, birth and death have no end; the long kalpa rushes on like a wheel, with no rest or pause. This is the reason for it. The Buddha taught all manner of methods for stilling the mind, yet every one of them is but a shim to stop the wheel. The Dharma-gates are many, but because beings are heavy with defilement and dull in consciousness, they are hard to gather in. Thus the single gate of Buddha-recitation is the most swift and essential. As it is said: who recollects the Buddha and recites the Buddha will, whether now or hereafter, surely see the Buddha. For all the deluded views of sentient beings belong to birth and death; only the view of seeing the Buddha is allowed as the dharma for escaping birth and death. Yet seeing the Buddha must come about through recollection and mindfulness. Deluded thoughts have no interval by day or night, and Buddha-recitation is deliberately used to cut them off. This is why Master Huiyuan established the White Lotus Society on Mount Lu and set up the water-clock for recitation six times a day. At that time only a hundred and twenty men were in the society, and those reckoned high worthies numbered but eighteen. So even genuine reciters of the Buddha were not many. That people today look on Buddha-recitation as the lowest rank of practice is surely not true understanding. In recent times only Niushan took Buddha-recitation as his practice, and moreover named it demon-smelting; but his tongs and hammer were too tight, and though he recited day and night without break, it lasted only the three winter months, and men are not all of one mold, so it could hardly be kept up long. Lately Yunqi strongly advocated Buddha-recitation; though he recited four periods a day, at night there was sleep, and much trouble was spent rousing the sleepers, so the method lacked subtlety and closeness. Now Master Foshi Xuanjin and his fellows have each made a vow, requesting the twelve-hour method. This method is indeed fine and close; yet in movement and stillness, eating and drinking, it seems hard to reduce it to one pattern. If it is regulated with due measure and arranged with skill, then it becomes a fine rule for ancient and modern alike. They asked the old man for instruction, and so I have drawn up regulations, that the business be not cumbrous and men’s minds come to one. This is a subtle and wondrous practice. And so I make the rule, with the articles set out below. In establishing a Buddha-recitation assembly, one follows the person and the vow; wide or narrow, it is not uniform. If one’s strength is great, then many halls; if one’s strength is slight, then one hall. People are the same. But no matter whether the number of people is many or few, they are evenly divided into six shifts; each shift by day and by night is two hours, rotating according to the incense. The shift on duty comes out to bow and recite, to walk the path and repent, while the rest all sit in silence, reciting inwardly as they hear, or practicing contemplation if they wish. Thus stillness is much and movement little, nothing is cumbrous and nothing confused, and the Buddha’s voice is unbroken, so deluded thoughts do not arise. It is like calling and answering one another: neither dull nor scattered. Entering, movement and stillness are one suchness; self and other are not two; waking and sleeping remain constant. Then one rises not from one’s seat and suddenly sees Amitabha. This is the first wish-fulfilling and wondrous practice. As for food and drink, it too should be regulated according to Dharma, so that inside and outside are one and the same; then self and other are both forgotten and right and wrong are wholly dissolved. And the peace and stillness of the practice-ground has no equal in wonder. The old man has pondered this method deeply, and is ashamed that his own feet have not yet found their footing there and his wish is not yet fulfilled. So I set it out especially, as a vanguard for others. In days to come, when those who see and hear are many, such halls will be established everywhere, and the Pure Land will spread throughout all China. This is what I hope for.

blocks.text: Terms for the Cultivation-and-Realization Assembly at the Zongjing Hall

inline.s: The Buddha set forth the whole canon of the Tripitaka, listing all practices in full, and gathering them all back into cultivation and realization as the ultimate end. As it is said, all myriad practices are established on the one mind, and by those myriad practices one returns to realize the one mind. Hence the saying: nothing that does not flow forth from this dharma-realm; nothing that does not return to this dharma-realm. Now the dharma-realm itself does not belong to delusion or enlightenment, to sage or ordinary being. It is only because of ignorance and non-awakening that this one mind is lost; from delusion heaping upon delusion, all sorts of karma are made, and one brings on oneself the suffering of rebirth and death. What is called cultivation and realization is simply cleansing the three obstructions of one’s own mind and restoring the original substance of one’s own mind; this is called realization. It is not that apart from cultivation there is some other realization. Therefore the essential instruction of the buddhas and patriarchs for those who cultivate is first to awaken to the one mind and cleanse the three obstructions. Because the mind is hard to awaken to, contemplative practice is set up to penetrate it; because the obstructions are hard to remove, repentance is set up to purify them. Even in the Huayan school’s perfect teaching of the dharma-realm, which honors Samantabhadra as the eldest son of Vairocana, among the ten kinds of kingly vows the confession of karmic obstructions stands first. Hence, from ancient times, even one who personally awakened to the Lotus Samadhi in the Tiantai tradition still honored the method of repentance as the wondrous practice, and ritual manuals were composed for it. Even Master Yongming, who belonged to the Pure Land fold, still reverently followed it and strove to practice it, how much more others. Alas, in this Dharma-Ending Age we are farther and farther from the sages; beings are heavy with defilement and their heaped delusion deeper and deeper. Having neither the work of awakening and investigation, nor the practice of repentance and confession of offenses, by what dharma can one hope to escape birth and death? Only Master Yongming melted down the whole canon and returned it to the purport of mind-only, composing a work in a hundred fascicles called the Zongjing Lu, and to this day his hall stands at Jingci. His book sets forth the one mind in full, like the sun and moon hung in the mid-sky, lighting up the depths of all dharmas. If a student can study it closely, he will see through to his own mind and need not seek further awakening. For entering realization, nothing surpasses it. In his own daily practice the Master recited the Lotus Sutra ten thousand times and held to the Tiantai Lotus repentance ritual, cultivating according to Dharma as his constant custom. Thus while he was yet alive in the world, the lord of the underworld had his portrait painted and paid it reverence, because his practice transcended birth and death and truly realized mind-only; such was the man. Now his book is still circulated and the hall still stands; who is there that passes by and asks about it? Here is Master Xuanjin He, his true heir. He left home as a child; on the day his head was shaved at that monastery he asked what sort of man the Master had been, and forthwith made a vow to pay homage at his stupa. Was he not perhaps one who had attended and served him in a former life? The Master’s stupa has long been buried and the hall ruined, yet this man could raise them up and restore them, so that the Master’s brow-light shines out again among mountains and rivers, grass and trees; this is not without cause. Now as conditions have gathered a little, this man vows to make clear the purport of the Zongjing and to devote himself to the work of repentance and realization. He will gather twelve true companions in Dharma and follow the model of the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra, vowing to make it a long-term practice. The year is divided into four seasons, and in each season twenty-one days are set aside for the repentance ritual according to the Lotus repentance manual. For the rest they daily read the Zongjing Lu to awaken to mind-only; when doubts arise, he explains the essential purport for the assembly, without branches and leaves, taking only what is direct and immediate as the root of investigation, hoping for true realization. He means to make those who enter the retreat the exemplars, and to lead the disciples of this mountain as fledgling meditators, trimming their wings that both may rise together in flight. In the vast emptiness of the Dharma-nature they will climb the heaven of enlightenment and brighten the sun of wisdom; this lies in the present undertaking. The terms of the retreat are arranged according to circumstances, seeking to be simple and easy to practice, true and without pretense, so as to tread the solid ground. Yet the four requisites cannot be provided by his own strength, for a summer retreat cannot follow the Tathagata’s rule of going begging each day, nor does he dare to hope for the manner of celestial beings sending offerings. So, matching name to reality, those who vow to supply them are looked for among lay patrons who have aroused the mind. Now the layman Tan Mengxun has taken the lead with all his strength, and so all who have affinity with it raise a cheer and respond. Since all dharmas arise from conditions, and the seed of Buddhahood arises from conditions, so this present condition, though near at hand, is in truth the first skillful means by which the far journey to Buddhahood is trodden. When the assembly heard this they rejoiced, and so the beginning was made; and the ultimate fruit rests with all of you of the same condition, same practice, same work, same mind, who rouse a single vigorous effort. If one exchanges a mind of worldly birth and death for a mind that transcends the world, and nourishes the life of samadhi and wisdom with wealth that only increases offenses, what wise man would hesitate to do it? But if one gives rise to a single doubting thought, then face to face one misses a hundred thousand million kalpas.
The Dream-Wandering Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Fascicle Forty-Seven
Author’s Preface to the Dream-Wandering Poetry Collection

The collection is called Dream-Wandering; what does the title mean? The three realms are a house of dreams; this floating life is a dream. Reversal and accord, suffering and joy, flourishing and withering, gain and loss, are all matters within a dream. As for its words, they record the scenes I wandered through in dreams, and poetry is what is most intimate in those scenes; in sum, all of it is dream-talk. Someone said: the Buddha forbids idle words; prose is already excessive, how much more poetry, which is the worst kind of idle words. Moreover, poetry is rooted in feeling, while Chan is the dharma that goes beyond feeling; would this not fall into the realm of feeling and thought? I replied: not so. The Buddha said that birth and death and nirvana are like a yesterday’s dream. Therefore the buddhas and patriarchs are also men in a dream, and the whole canon and the seventeen hundred koans are nothing but dream-talk; why should this be the exception? Monks who made poetry began with Zhidun and Huiyuan in the Jin; by the Tang there were more than thirty sons of Sakyamuni; in the early years of our Ming there were Chushi, Jianxin, Jitan, Yichu and other great elders; after that nothing was heard. In the Jiajing and Longqing eras, when I was a boy, I knew of one Yuzhi of Qiantang, but his poems were not transmitted. In Jiangnan it began with me and Xuelang. Xuelang was deeply addicted to it and traveled all over the Sanwu region among famous masters, polishing and discussing without a moment’s pause, so that his fame stirred a whole age. I, being sunk in withered Chan, early laid down brush and inkstone, and went wandering with one bowl; and keeping silence in empty mountains I spat out all my old habits, leaving not a single character in my breast. From Mount Wutai to the Eastern Sea, through twenty years, sometimes the old habit burst out fiercely, and the drafts were thrown away as they came. Now I am fifty. It happened that for spreading the Dharma I met with calamity and was sent down to prison by imperial decree, close to nine deaths; afterward by grace I was exiled to the passes and the seas. This I took as a dream of falling into a perilous road, and so these words were first preserved. For I saw that the best of ancient poems mostly came from men on garrison duty and long sojourners far from home, because their feeling is true and their circumstances real. Moreover, monks who followed the garrisons are rarely seen in any age: at the end of the Tang there was Guquan, in the Song there were Dahui and Juefan, two men, and in the Ming there was only myself. Guquan died in the army; what was handed down from him was only a single verse at the end, which said: Today is the sixth of the sixth month; Guquan’s punishment is complete. If not to heaven above, then into hell below. When he had spoken he passed away. Dahui was moved to Meiyang and gave expression to Chan sayings; there is the Arsenal of the Chan School. Juefan was banished to Zhuyai and produced his Surangama Peak Treatise. Not much of their poetry is recorded either. I am ashamed that in the Way I am not equal to these former worthies, yet what I met with surpassed theirs, and the time lasted longer, and my circumstances were not as theirs. In the second month of spring in the bing-shen year I first arrived at the garrison post; for three years there were plague and famine, and white bones covered the fields. I sat as though in a charnel grove, and feared that I might die and leave no record. So I completed my Notes on the Lankavatara Sutra. Holding a halberd at the great general’s gate, dwelling among the ramparts, I thought to imitate Dahui in teaching the Dharma in cap and kerchief. I built a ten-foot room within a domed tent, and from time to time with the disciples who came I performed dream-illusion Buddha-work: gongs and drums for bells and chimes, banners and flags for streamers and canopies, the watch-drum for my alms bowl, the long spear for my staff, the three armies for my companions in Dharma, the ranks of soldiers for the pure regulations, their war cries for the sound of the tide, their formal visits for bowing and recitation, and all the demons for my family. It was, after all, a great practice-ground. Hence what I spoke, whether Dharma talks or verses of praise, was mostly supramundane, while the poems were spoken especially to accord with the world. Though I did not ascend the Dharma hall, sit on the jeweled seat, raise the mallet or lift the whisk, yet dwelling amid toil, mingling with worldly truth, I suddenly entered the gate of non-duality, in no way inferior to Vimalakirti — only lacking one heaven-dwelling flower-scatterer. My words are impure because the listeners were not of one kind; they are medicine answering the disease, and of themselves have nothing to do with the buddhas’ and patriarchs’ upward gate. In truth they are one strange stretch of dream-illusion conditions within the Dharma-gate over a thousand years. When by grace I was restored to my former robes and went to Mount Heng and Mount Lu, it was again like wandering in dream to Mount Tianmu. Over twenty years my attendant Fushan accumulated them day by day, and my disciple Tongjiong, who lived with me at Wuru, arranged them into fascicles. When people asked for them I did not dare bring them out, fearing to stain the pure realm. Haiyin, a disciple of Yangshan in Xin’an, asked that the poems be carved and printed first in order. I know that seen with waking eyes they are like bird tracks in cold sky and fish traces in autumn water; if one seeks them in words and letters, they are flowers in a cataract-clouded eye, and in the end one cannot escape speaking of dreams within a dream. Written on the Lantern Festival, the first month of spring in the xin-you year, the first year of Tianqi, by the idle old man of Mount Kuang, Old Man Hanshan, the monk Deqing, in the Withered-Wood Hut.
Ten Poems on the Journey, Each in Four Lines

The soaring goose of heaven flies,
And as it flies it cries.
It calls with piteous voice,
Lamenting this long enterprise.

The fire-clouds stream like water,
The white sun is an arrow.
My far march brings no return —
Does anyone remember?

I bathe my ears in the spring,
And wild ferns ease my hunger.
Not that I have no heart —
What manner of man are you?

The purple mushrooms bloom,
The white stones glisten bright.
Far off the one I long for —
I wake until the light.

Who says a drop of water
Can wear the stone away?
Who says one may forget one’s grief?
My heart is woven day by day.

The sun may well grow cold,
The wind be tied and stilled;
But sorrow rises from within,
And whence it comes, unfilled.

The tall pines stand and stand,
Where apes and cranes abide.
The white clouds drift and drift —
My heart has gone with the tide.

Hunger and thirst are mine,
Food and drink come light.
I sigh for that drunken fellow —
Hard it is to stay clear-eyed.

There is wine, and it is fine;
Truly it is for friends.
But dark and silent all —
The cups have long been dry.

Alas, you traveler,
Who come and go and greet:
Ask him why he wanders —
No one knows his reason.
Fifteen Poems on the Times, Each in Four Lines (with Preface)

I have lately heard that in all quarters there have been floods and droughts for years together, and on top of that a plague of locusts. The people live in terror, not waiting for evening to come upon morning. The officials petitioned to inform the throne, and the imperial compassion took pity on them. The public treasuries within and without all sent out gold and grain for relief, and the hundred ministers, admiring this virtue, each donated a year’s salary to assist. Such a thing has never been before. Moved by it, I made these poems.

Heaven loves all living things —
Why then this cruel blow?
The people seek but peace —
Why will it not be so?

The surging waters rose;
Yu tamed the flood and tide.
But when the rains run wild,
Who then can turn the tide?

Sweet dew falls thick and kind,
Timely rain like broth.
Not one small cloud will rise —
The people live in dread.

The rains have missed their season;
The people are worn and spent.
And worse, the drought-fiend comes —
How cruel is its intent.

Locusts blot out the sky;
Why must it be this way?
They gnaw the fat and marrow,
And leave the people in dismay.

What the people hold most dear
Is food, more than father and mother;
To trade one’s child for food —
That saying is bitter indeed.

The heaven of the sovereign
Loves the people of this land.
The people’s very lives
Rest in the sovereign’s hand.

Vast is the sovereign’s grace:
Gold and grain he bestows.
Who can spit water forth
And make the sky rain grain?

By reverencing Heaven,
Rain and shine come in season.
By pitying the people,
His gifts exceed all reason.

The means to reward merit
Belongs to Heaven above.
Were they not our own kind,
Who would bestow such love?

Far off in high antiquity
The fine grain grew untilled.
Alas for these last days —
Sowing brings no yield.

Wretched things that live and crawl,
I am one with them all.
The sovereign Heaven on high —
I bear it with them all.

If only the earth were fat
And spared the people’s toil.
If only the Yellow Emperor
Would let them eat and rest.

The people of the broad highway
Are never lacking anywhere.
The transforming rule of Yao —
Who says it does not last?

The times have gone their way,
And cannot be pulled back.
The people’s suffering is here —
It cannot be delayed.
Singing of My Heart (Written in the Garden)
Receiving a Vegetarian Feast at the Pure Land Hermitage in Luling from Layman Wang Xinghai, and Thereby Thinking of Magistrate Wang

A single grain of rice from Luling
Is worth more than Mount Sumeru.
Sumeru may yet be shattered,
But this grain has no time of ruin.

It turns into fragrant rice,
And becomes provision for the Pure Land.
Picked up and eaten just as it comes,
One meal forgets a hundred hungers.

Like eating diamond dust —
Never digested, it passes through the skin.
In this land are many lotuses,
And all kinds of wondrous fragrance spread.

One person sits on each flower,
Left and right they follow one another.
Their radiance outshines the sun and moon;
A finger-snap transcends asamkhya kalpas.

And yet one seat among the flowers is empty —
Long, long it keeps my thoughts in labor.
Joyfully Meeting Old Man Wang Tangnan Again in Luling (with Introduction)

When I was twenty-five I once visited Qingyuan and met the old gentleman, who was then fifty. Now I have met him again, and more than half that span has passed. It seems but yesterday. Because the old gentleman has purified his mind in pure karma, his complexion is like a baby’s. Moved by the past and thinking of the present, I rejoice and write this gift.

A human life of a hundred years,
Divided in four, is twenty-five.
At our first meeting he was half of half;
At this second, half of ten.

You have already passed three parts,
Yet you look just as when first seen.
Your face wears a baby’s color;
Your bones are like a diamond shaft.

Your thought is set on entering the lotus;
Your voice comes forth as a heavenly drum.
You sit upright on the seven-jeweled terrace,
And walk among the trees of many fragrances.

Never leaving the body of the five aggregates,
And yet this is the land of purity.
Smash the kalavinka bottle —
And you shall see the lord within the flower.

Though I am parted from you,
This is exactly where we meet.
Six Poems

When the golden-winged garuda dies,
Its flesh and bones all scatter away.
Only the mind does not dissolve —
Perfect and bright, its radiance blazing.

The dragon king takes it for a pearl,
And it breaks through every darkness.
The wheel-turning king gains the wish-fulfilling gem,
And can rescue every hardship.

How is it that among men
It is used all day and never seen?
Impermanence

The Dharma-nature is itself impermanent,
Yet it does not fall among the categories.
It is like clouds within the sky —
In its very substance it abides forever.

Sages and ordinary beings are all passing guests;
Coming and going, there are no two roads.
Is this birth, or is it no birth?
Neither new nor old.

The one whose wisdom-eye sees clearly —
What else could he long for beyond this?

In a dream I entered a mass of raging fire,
Terrified and full of panic.
Just when suffering pressed hardest,
A drop of water brought coolness.

The water gone, the fire burned again —
What use to long and sigh?
And when at last I looked with waking eyes,
Who was it, there, that grieved?

Mount Sumeru spans the vast void;
The great earth floats on the fragrant sea.
The six dusts blind the heaven of our nature;
The four elements pervade the dharma-realm.

When the kalpa-fire blazes forth,
Will this one be destroyed or not?
Why wait for it to burn itself out,
And only then be without obstruction?
No-Self

One water takes on every taste —
Sour, salt, bitter, pungent, all.
Because its own nature is bland,
It can accomplish all these things.

If it truly did not follow,
Why would it go along with them?
Only one who does not follow —
Who can know this flavor?
Birth and Death

Birth and death do not flow on;
What flows on is not birth and death.
If in truth there were no flowing,
Birth and death would never end.

Truly observe the nature of flowing —
The flowing stops at once.
When the flowing mind is not seen,
This is truly escaping birth and death.
Ballad of Bitter Heat

The world suffers under burning heat;
Why is my heart so cool?
Simply because there is nothing it can touch —
And so it rests as always.

It is like cloth washed in fire:
The more it is tried, the more it shines.
Look at those petty souls —
Who among them could face such a thing?
Crossing the Three Gorges on a Moonlit Night
Four Poems Longing for the Pure Land

Alas for this land of endurance,
Where men are made of many cares.
When sorrow comes, a hundred thoughts knot up,
And busily they drive the body on.

All sufferings gather in this petty frame,
As rotting flesh draws the bluebottle flies.
Befuddled, they do not know themselves,
Toiling and scurrying from dawn to dusk.

Their purity diminishes day by day;
Submerged, they wear out body and spirit.
How can they wash away the filth of passion,
And in one turn return to what is real?

Then they would bow farewell to the burning house,
And take their leave of the world’s clamor,
Roaming at ease in the land of purity,
Whose joy has no bound at all.

I have heard that in the far west
There is a land named Ultimate Bliss.
Wondrously adorned are its palaces,
With jeweled nets and pearl-strung threads.

Gods and men gather there in crowds,
Their radiance outshining one another.
In the gardens bloom a hundred flowers;
Heavenly music scatters through the air.

Lotuses open in the pool of eight virtues;
Fragrance drifts about the seven-jeweled towers.
A soft breeze blows at the eaves,
And golden bells resound among the clouds.

All manner of birds sing in harmony,
Pouring out the sounds of Dharma.
Once mortal ears have heard them,
All are freed upon the spot.

Ultimate Bliss is not far off —
Say instead: a hundred thousand million lands.
If one can but make one thought pure,
It appears before the eyes just as it is.

Lotuses are born from the mud of desire;
Coolness springs up from blazing flame.
Tiles and pebbles become jade and jasper;
The jeweled grove rises from brambles.

The knotted thought blocks off mountains and rivers;
Dissolve the thought, and darkness is broken.
The perilous road becomes a level highway;
The root of passion realizes the first ground.

Who knows that within the subtle and secret
Both purity and filth, both suffering and joy, are complete?
Just look at the flowers in the empty air —
Their rising and perishing has no bound.

Suffering is born of hate and love;
Joy is won from purity and stillness.
It is like a man in a dream:
Noble or base, he seeks nothing outside.

Passion and thought have no beginning;
Suffering and joy are not foreordained.
Look at the clouds in the clear sky —
In an instant they change and vanish.

The foolish cling to them as real,
Chasing circumstances in toil of joy and grief.
The wise man prizes clear illumination,
And wipes away the old habits of delusion.

Once awakened, he is never deluded again;
His spirit’s deep spring stays forever still.
May I ride the white-rayed light,
And sit upright in the land of Ultimate Bliss.
Song of Pearl-Diving

The blazing bright moon-pearl
Is born at the bottom of the deep.
They snatch it from the empty water,
And all the fish and dragons start up in fright.

The merman and mermaid embrace and weep;
Their falling tears turn suddenly to rain.
A rank wind strikes the far shore;
Whale-waves run ten thousand miles.

Fine nets hang down like clouds of sky;
Light sails spread like the peng-bird’s wings.
One cut, and the river’s queen is grieved;
A second blow, and the sea-god moves away.

They split open every oyster’s belly,
Yet cannot mend the people’s marrow.
If only there were a wish-fulfilling pearl
To carry home and offer to the Son of Heaven.

Its holy light would shine at midnight,
And the dragon countenance would greatly rejoice.
The seven treasures would follow every wish;
The four seasons would all be rich and fine.

Then it would be passed on to relieve the orphaned and poor,
Benefiting and gladdening without end.
And it would reward the merit of victory in war,
Handed down as a blessing of consecration.

So the toil of provoking the dragon would be ended,
To ease at last the smiting of their thighs.
The vast sea would no longer raise its waves;
The ditches would be clear of mud and silt.

May I wish long life to our sovereign,
Its measure equal to the waters of the eastern sea.
Singing of the Dragon
Singing of the Tiger
Given to a Wandering Monk of Caoxi (with Introduction)

The surveillance commissioner of Nanxiong and Shaozhou, Lord Zhu, had scarcely arrived at his post when he was pierced with grief at the desolation of the ancestral court, and did all in his power to set it in order, even taking for himself the name of Wandering Monk of Caoxi. Moved by this, I wrote and gave him these lines.

The Caoxi wanderer comes,
And to Caoxi he goes.
Long borrowed and never returned,
He suddenly recalls the road to Caoxi.

Then he falls into a magistrate’s form,
Yet still he dwells nowhere at all.
Carried on in the great transformation,
What net could ever bind him?

I still recall the words at parting:
Bodhi is fundamentally no tree.
By this he is not deluded,
And everywhere he finds awakening.

Following conditions he comes to his old home,
Where ten thousand mountains brim with mist and cloud.
Before he enters Caoxi’s gate,
His mind is already as of old.

How much more when he sees the men of former days —
Sadly he pours out his inmost heart.
He lifts up the robe handed down,
As though it were first entrusted to him.

He smashes the stone that fell and crushed the waist,
And opens wide the storehouse of treasure,
Drawing out the wish-fulfilling pearl,
Boasting alone in the elder’s wealth.

The three carts are given out as each requires,
And the children are suddenly struck with awe.
One shout brings ghosts and gods to tears;
One phrase drives off the foxes and hares.

The mountain goblins at once hide their tracks;
Dragons and serpents joyfully interweave.
He walks within the field of stillness,
Coming and going on staff and sandals.

He pierces through the clouds at the ravine’s bottom,
And treads dry the dew on the tips of grass.
Even tiles and pebbles shine with light;
The sacred source is never dried.

Who knows the earlier and later bodies?
Host and guest look at one another.
May I grasp the goad of skillful means,
And drive the white ox onward at a long pace.
Answering Secretary Dong Chongxiang, Who Visited Me at Caoxi
The Gentlemen of the Green Locust Society Came to Inquire After Me; I Was Keeping Retreat and Did Not Meet Them, So I Showed Them This

Within the blazing burning house,
There is one patch of coolness.
Though the gift came from an elder,
It is in truth the sovereign’s bestowal.

My companions in Dharma gladly came,
And their high hearts opened hidden depths.
They saw through to the mind before a word was spoken,
And reached straight to the unborn intent.

Why need one ask of Vimalakirti?
Herein is true non-duality.
Grand Secretary Dong Xuanzai Painted a Mountain Scene and Gave It to Me on My Way to Leiyang; I Wrote This in Reply
On My Birthday in the Gui-mao Year, Written on the Boat from Wuyang to Caoxi

Today I am fifty-eight;
Tomorrow, fifty-nine.
What is to come cannot be conceived;
What is past — what is there left?

The marks of the world are flowers in the air;
Praise and blame are ugliness in a mirror.
I do not press on with the sheep-cart or deer-cart;
I am glad to follow where ox and horse go.

I am ashamed my knees wore through the rush mat;
Yet I wonder that a willow grows from my elbow.
My hair is loose, with few caps to bind it;
My face is thick with dust and grime.

I have fought back the army of birth and death,
And smashed the mortar of ignorance.
I have spent all a fond old woman’s heart,
And laughed the empty sky’s mouth wide open.

Since neither shore will have me,
And midstream is no place to stand,
Coming and going I let the wind and waves,
And in going or staying I keep no mate.

At the sky’s edge I gaze toward Chang’an,
And in the cold sky turn my head once.
Turning my head, I ask the men of the time:
Who among you is a friend of mine?
Visiting Fangguang Temple

At dawn I parted the clouds of the Southern Marchmount;
At dusk I lodged at Fangguang Temple.
One steep and winding path runs deep;
A thousand peaks lock in their hidden secrets.

Sitting solemn as on a blue lotus,
I suddenly enter the land of coolness.
The flowing spring blends with the sound of pines,
As though conversing in non-duality.

Only cut off the worldly mind —
Do not ask about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming.
How could I settle here on a branch,
To fulfill my wish to dwell in the mountains?

Let this banana-body rest,
And spit out the affair of flowers in the air.
From now on I take leave of the dust of the world,
Forever ending the entanglements of a living man.
Roaming the Southern Marchmount and Climbing Zhurong Peak

I have cherished the Southern Marchmount
In dream and thought for forty years.
Its seventy peaks at the sky’s edge
Have always stood before my eyes.

I am ashamed to have no wings,
And worse, to be bound by this form.
But lately I kept an old friend’s tryst,
And at last could roam and wander freely.

Gathering my robe I climbed Zhurong,
And gazed out over the empty Chu skies.
The Xiang River stretched like a bolt of white silk;
The stars and Dipper hung about my waist.

From heaven there was less than a foot;
In a daze I followed the flying immortals.
Looking askance, all things were small;
The world was a pellet for a crossbow.

The body had entered emptiness;
Beneath my feet floated clouds and mist.
If I could ride the cold wind away,
I would rise beyond the dusty world.

Turning my head I think of the men of old —
What bond was there across three lives?
A single drop of water from Caoxi
Became a soaking rain of blessing,
Waking the withered sprout of spirit,
And the Dharma-drum roused the sleeping and the fallen.

How is it that in the lion’s den
Foxes and hares now lurk?
The monasteries stand empty and still;
The lamp of wisdom is dim and unlit.

Who will hold up the torch that lights the heavens,
And break the long night’s sleep?
Pacing to and fro I turn more sorrowful,
My tears flowing like a spring.

If only I had great spiritual power,
To snap my fingers and transform the trichiliocosm,
Turning it at once into a land of seven treasures,
Strewn everywhere with golden lotuses,
So that one might see the clouds in the sky,
And all the sages and worthies gather round.
Parting from the Southern Marchmount Hermit Kuang Muyi

I came from Caoxi,
Meaning to grow old among the mountains.
The mountain spirit did not deceive me;
Clouds and sunset glow filled my eyes.

I visited the ancient practice-grounds,
Where gold sand fell among thick bamboos.
The place where Lazy Can roasted his taro —
Its hidden traces can no longer be traced.

Far off I think of the master who polished bricks;
He was slow to become a Buddha, to his cost.
The king within the lion’s den —
Who dares lay a hand on his claws?

The Dharma-rain has long not moistened;
The sprout of spirit has withered after all.
Alas that I came so late;
Facing the wind I am only more vexed.

But I am fortunate to meet a cloud-eating man,
With whom I may look beyond the world.
I would sit with him in a deep ravine,
And exhaust the subtle mysteries of dark words.

I love this lofty mind of his,
Which truly can renounce all confusion.
Yet the Lotus Society has not yet opened,
And I must take the eastward road again.

Truly, because of the bonds of kin,
My heart is long wound about with care.
Now I take a brief leave of cloud and mountain,
But this heart will never be settled.

I board the boat on the river;
You hide like a leopard in the mountains.
And I think of Li Yehou —
I fear your leisure will not long be safe.

Only let the cloud before your window stay,
And wait for me to sweep it when I return.
Leaving for the Eastern Journey on the River from the Southern Marchmount, Parting with Fang Juezhi

I met you on the river,
And planned to make our home in the hills.
We pledged to lie down together in white clouds,
And there grow old side by side.

The mountain spirit would not keep me;
I dragged my staff and left the deep recesses.
You too are weary of wandering,
Your will set beyond mist and sunset glow.

Your spirit is hidden in the gate of all mysteries;
Long have you wished to renounce confusion.
But your heart is tied to those you owe your life to,
And you cannot yet do as your heart desires.

Now I steer the boat of compassion,
And raise sail across the vast and boundless.
Though I am parted from you,
Our affinity is still not finished.

If I am granted years not yet exhausted,
I shall pick up a single blade of grass again.
Wait only until your children are married;
It will still be early when you return.
Parting from Mount Heng: A Self-Mocking Piece

Lying in the empty forest did not hold me firm;
Once more I set in order my eastward boat.
Dimly I take leave of cloud and mountain,
Deeply entangled, my heart wound about.

The seventy peaks of Mount Heng —
Long have I wished to explore their recesses.
I had but come, and now I go at once,
Leaving the mountain spirit to mock me.

My return was already late;
Why then is my parting so early?
I am by nature a man of the mountains;
Hills and valleys have long since filled me.

My staff and sandals breed mist and cloud;
Sitting or lying, deer and elk surround me.
Eye and ear will not admit dust;
The light of mind is beyond dusk and dawn.

The four elements are like an empty valley;
The six senses are cut off from all confusion.
Wherever I am is a deep mountain —
Why must I cling to this withered place?

Let me ask the men within the mountains:
When will the bonds of stillness ever end?
Smash the crystal bottle —
Then you will know the good of following conditions.
Meeting the Two Chan Monks Shilang and Minyue at Wuchang, Who Were Returning to Shu to See Their Parents; Shown to Them

I am myself a wandering monk,
And suddenly I meet a wandering guest.
I ask him about the affair of wandering —
We look at each other and say not a word.

One patch of cloud on Mount Kuang,
A thousand feet of snow on Mount Emei —
This is the wandering mind:
Coming and going, the moon in the water.

And so I think of a mother’s and child’s love;
Thought after thought, they are not cut off.
Now you go home to gladden their faces,
As though you had never parted.

You serve the decree, not the sweet;
You ask after the cold, not the heat.
Split open the face your mother bore —
Then you will see the unborn and undying.

This is what a wandering monk is,
And this is the season of coming home.
Shown to Wen Ziyu in His Illness

Illness arises from there being a self;
The self is gathered by affliction.
Affliction is fed by craving and delusion;
Birth and death wheel on without rest.

The root of passion is like a shuttle;
Deluded thoughts weave in and out,
Weaving the body of illusion and delusion,
Where all sufferings heap up together.

To seek the skillful means of escaping suffering,
Swing the sword of wisdom at once.
Cut through the thread of deluded thought —
Root and object are still on the spot.

One thought awakens to no-birth;
The four elements each return to their own.
If the self cannot be found,
Where will you go looking for illness?
Returning to Mount Kuang (with Introduction)

In youth I set my heart on distant wandering; at thirty I dwelt in the mountains, and in a flash twenty years passed. Suddenly the wind of karma blew me into the sea of illusion, and for more than twenty years this one thought has never left the ice and snow of the cold cliff. Lately I have been fortunate to return late to Mount Kuang, to spend my old age there. I am now seventy-two. Alas, alas, this floating world — how long is a human life? Looking at this remnant of life is like the setting sun in the western hills, its floating light gone in a breath. So I made a poem to record it.

This floating world holds not a hundred years;
My dream-wandering has passed seventy.
The sea of illusion stretches in vast waves;
The other shore has no direction or corner.

A single reed follows the wind of heaven,
Drifting wherever it will.
I have traveled all round the eight wastes;
The perils were not of one kind only.

My spirit is weary and my strength spent;
I erase my traces and plan a distant course.
Mist and sunset glow knit my dreams;
My heart has long wronged the cliff and cave.

Only in declining years did I fulfill my wish,
And shake my sleeves to return to Mount Kuang.
Once beyond the ties of the muddy world,
All thoughts are utterly dried up.

The thousand peaks embrace their hidden ravines,
Far removed from the world of men.
The Seven Worthies stand ranged in the clouds;
The Five Elders beckon me again and again.

Their brows and eyes face me from time to time;
Whistling and singing, there is much delight.
The bright moon comes when it will,
A single mirror hung in the void.

Its clear light enters my thatched hut,
And shines on me, and my face eases.
White hair faces the blue mountains;
Body and shadow are like an ice jar.

Slumped, I squat on a stone couch,
Cross-legged day and night.
Turning back to look before I was born,
Originally there was not a single thing.

Clearly knowing the conditions of illusion,
Why be bound by this life?
From now on I am freed from tangles,
And climb high to the city of lasting joy.
Sent to Grand Secretary Qian Shouzhi

Mount Kuang stands ranged in the clouds;
Rivers and lakes stretch to the sky’s edge.
Blue lotuses spring from the earth,
Their leaves and branches fresh and fair.

I think fondly of the man within those flowers,
Standing beyond the dusty world.
For fifty years I have dreamed of him,
But the good affinity has never come to pass.

By chance I rode a cloud in the sky,
And came with the wind to Wu.
The southeast has fine mountains and waters,
And many worthy men to wake and lean upon.

At one meeting with a man of plain heart,
My spirit was as though drunk.
Before words, our inmost hearts were poured out;
Our pure talk entered the finest subtleties.

Face to face we forgot our bodies,
And clearly were freed from all restraint.
A pure white supramundane mind —
By the vast void it can truly be sworn.

The sea of suffering is just now in great waves;
I would speak of ferrying across.
We take our leave at the river bridge,
And so I fulfill my will to return to the hills.

With a deep bow I go back to Mount Kuang,
Hiding my traces in the deep and secret.
The Five Elders and the Seven Worthies
I face and gaze on day and night.

I cut thatch and lie down in the empty mountain,
With mist and sunset glow for clothing.
This banana-body I look on
And cast away like spittle.

I think longingly of the man who has not returned,
My feelings racing, toiling in dreams.
If only I could ride a long rainbow,
And come to him suddenly on the wind.

For a while to take leave of the world’s ties,
And enter my true samadhi.
At Guizong, Climbing Gold Wheel Peak and Paying Homage at the Relic Stupa

I climbed Gold Wheel Peak,
And one glance made heaven and earth narrow.
The crowd of mountains ran like ants;
Peng Lake was small as a leaf.

Ten thousand ravines roared with the long wind,
Blowing down the moon from the sky’s edge.
In the still night I looked down below,
Where lamps and fires flickered on and off.

The body entered emptiness at one stroke,
And all thoughts suddenly came to rest.
Far off I recall the World-Honored One who saves the world,
Whose Dharma-body pervades all things.

The relics came from the west;
The great being spread the three karmas.
On the peak top he raised a stupa,
Adorned with gold and iron.

And so he moved a great man
To build the monastery and give up his dwelling,
Which became a banner of light,
And the Dharma-affinity was knit from then on.

Above and below for more than a thousand years
It has brought coolness and dispelled the heat.
Alas for the realm of sentient beings:
The four marks turn into a kalpa of ruin.

The Chan palace has fallen to brambles;
Its gold and azure have become rubble.
The grove has met the axe;
Only one pine stands alone, towering.

Its root and trunk are half stripped and broken;
Its branches and boughs are about to snap.
Who would have thought a true man would come,
And with mantric vows bestow rich moisture?

By this we divine a great revival;
The Dharma-thunder will shake the worthies of old.
Bark and bone grow day and night,
And dense and flourishing it returns to life.

Fruit fulfilled in the diamond mind,
The wasteland is opened from now on.
The Dharma-storehouse comes down from heaven;
Dragon light shines on cliff and cave.

The monasteries rise like clouds,
And the four assemblies increase in joy.
Then we know that pure and impure lands
Change only as the mind inclines.
Donglin: Thinking of the Past
Poems on What I Have Met, Respectfully Answering Magistrate Yuan of Nankang (with Introduction)

Lord Yuan of Jiuji governed the prefecture of Nankang. The hills and lakes south of Mount Kuang all came under his transforming care. Not only did the people there bear his virtue; even the men of the cliffs and caves seemed to sit upright within his white-rayed presence. The ancient monastery of Qixian had long lain in wild thickets, and in one stroke he raised and renewed it; he also built the Cloud-Piercing Bridge to relieve a perilous road. These are imperishable triumphs for this famous mountain. The opening of the Dharma-cloud truly was moved by the protector of the Dharma’s single-hearted resolve. I received the gift of a record of the monastery, whose every word is enough to hand down a thousand years; I had it carved in stone to announce completion, and offer these rustic lines in thanks.

Mount Kuang rises high into the clouds;
Heaven and earth concentrate their fine spirit there.
A thousand peaks stand ranged in the highest heavens;
Blue lotuses crowd the sky’s edge.

In former times many cloud-eating men
Hid their forms and nourished hidden mysteries.
From the time Master Huiyuan came,
And opened the grove and knit true bonds,
High worthies gathered like clouds,
Purifying themselves in hope of transcending the world.

Mountain colors mirror the lake’s light;
Man and scene charm one another.
I recall the company of dragon-elephants,
Dharma-banners ranged like a marketplace.
I think fondly of that old man of Qixian,
Whose tongue was like a boiling cauldron.

In the moment between mallet and whisk,
He pointed straight at the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming.
Who would have thought that a thousand years later
The wheel of transformation would quietly turn?

The jeweled steps have fallen into wild thickets;
The heavens’ palaces sink into thorns.
Though the elder picked one blade of grass,
He grasped no truth by it.
How much less the howling of the jackal,
Which cannot match the lion’s play.

Bell and chime are silent;
The mountain is empty and the ghosts weep.
Then Heaven lent us a true man,
Who had received the prophecy on Vulture Peak.
He manifests the body of a magistrate,
And does the Buddha’s work as conditions allow.

The Dharma-rain moistens the scorched and withered;
Sweet showers enrich the hundred plants.
One patch of diamond mind
Is spread wide as the great earth.

The people are like infants,
And he a loving mother watching over them.
He spits out his food and tastes no sweetness;
He blends the remedy and removes what is harmful.

Whatever lies within his pointing and glance
Is seldom left without provision.
A thousand miles sit in the spring wind;
No dog barks in the neglected villages.

The teeming folk with teeth in their mouths
Are set as in the days of Getian.
In leisure from government he has many quiet moods;
He seeks the mountains and explores their wonders.

Seeing this Jetavana grove,
He is moved and rouses the will to restore it.
One lift of his craftsman’s hand,
And the red rafters spread like clouds on wings.

In no time the Brahma palace is complete,
As though it had come down from heaven.
His sacred power still has something left,
As if the adornment were not yet complete.

Across the sheer ravine he throws a flying bridge,
A long rainbow belted with dark green.
The jade pool lies with its dragon coiled,
Its form and shadow seeming to look back.

The Five Elders and the Seven Worthies
Let their beards and brows fall from the clouds.
On the perilous road he sets the boat of compassion,
So that travelers need not stumble.

I think longingly of his grace in aiding and ferrying;
It is not confined within one region.
Whenever I catch the remnant of his speech,
Jade dust falls on my liver and lungs.

Fine jasper is carved into noble lines;
A single stone entrusts them to bell and cauldron.
His merit is recorded on this famous mountain;
Lord Kuang should be ranked among its sacrifices.

Woodcutters’ songs join the Brahma sound,
Chanting blessings for a thousand myriad years.
The empty valley heaps up clouds and sunset glow,
All of them vessels of offering.

Moved by this rare affinity in the world,
I have written a short song to set out my heart.
May I speak a wish for his long life,
Forever bestowed on gods and men.
Somewhere in My Thoughts
Song on Looking at Hou Sheng’s Painting of Mountains and Waters
Song of the Udumbara Hermitage, Presented to the Historian of the Jetavana Grove, General Du Taoying
Song of the Wooden Hut (with Introduction)
The Chan monk Jingtai changed his style-name to Mu’an, the Wooden Hut. Layman Nan of Ben made him a gift of verse, and so I wrote this in play.
The Crow Cries at Night

In the cold wood the piled snow lies, the white sun in the west;
The kindly crow caws hoarsely from the branch,
While the owl in its nest dares not yet roost.
Hungry and with nothing to eat, its plight is piteous.

The fowler’s nets and snares are set how thick!
The flesh of a hungry crow is not worth eating.
Why then weave and plot and seek it day and night?
Its young cannot be fed, and its grief has no end.

Mother and child are parted, neither whole;
And worse, the mother dies and goes to the Yellow Springs.
Its crying never ceases, like the cuckoo’s;
And the orphan bears its grief for all its days.

Crow, crying crow, you are truly pitiable —
But the fowler suddenly died and the owl was slain.
Bright, bright is the way of Heaven, and how manifest!
Song of Roaming Mount Fu

An island in the air gathers the blue sunset glow,
Just like a lotus floating on the fragrant sea.
Cliff caves and stone grottoes cluster like flower stamens,
And again like Indra’s net with its crossing pearls.

I come and climb from afar to the realm of the lotus treasury;
Once my two eyes open there is no obstruction.
All around, the rows of trees cast shadow upon shadow,
Bright and clear as a mustard seed in a jar.

Halls and pavilions span the sky, shadows in the clouds;
The Dharma-body does not move, stable as the blue hills.
Flying flower-fragrance drifts with hidden scent,
Breathing on a man till his thick robe grows cold.

I drag my staff and part the mist within the cliffs;
Strange rocks jut up like a chessboard spread.
Pointing them out, they are like the ranked stars;
One spray of spittle spatters the blue sky.

The stone gate and its steps run in a single thread;
Turning sideways on the half-cliff, a foot has no room.
Even apes and birds find it hard to pass —
How then shall my own strength not be spent?

Clutching vines I climb straight to the wondrous peak;
Below my eyes the lake’s light spreads brocade of glow.
My feet have not left the ground, yet my body holds the void;
Looking back it is like a shadow in an ice jar.

Turning a little, I pass on to Huisheng Cliff;
What a wonder are its stone corridors and chambers.
The far ancestor excelled at teaching Dharma by the chessboard;
Before black and white appeared, he set men guessing.

Crossing the stream and going west, I reach Lotus Rock;
Golden lotuses bloom one by one from the ground.
I linger, but see no one among the flowers;
I only hear the pine wind’s broad and long tongue.

I bow in return to the sixteen-foot golden body in the Golden Valley,
Void and bright, with no room for the least dust.
When the kalpa-fire blazes, this will not be destroyed;
Then I believe the gray cliff is the original truth.

I would cut thatch and live beside this stone chamber,
And hide my traces here for the rest of my life.
If I could but sleep in peace while the white sun climbs high,
Body, mind and world I would cast all away.

Why should I leave this place and go elsewhere?
A single leaf floating in the void is nothing but a lodging.
Better to hurry and come home before long,
And not make the apes and cranes pine for me.

The lotus treasury has always been my old home;
Travel the ten directions to the end, you cannot leave it.
Hide yourself and enter at once into one mote of dust —
Who here knows the news of it?
Song of the Board-Carrying Man (with Introduction)

The Dharma cave of Mount Jing: since Dahui, the Way of Linji has continued without a break in its wisdom-life, and each generation has had its men. Lately the Chan gate has fallen desolate, and its echoes have long ceased. Of late a number of seekers have sat filling the mountain, and some among them have had a moment of insight, seen the truth before them, and won great freedom. Yet alas, they sit down on that white, clean ground and will not let it go, taking it for something extraordinary, unaware that it has instead become a Dharma-obstruction. In the teachings it is called the obstruction of the known. So the ancients said: even if you reach the point of a cold pool’s bright moon or a still night’s temple bell — struck, and it does not fail; touched by waves, and it is not scattered — this is still a matter on the shore of birth and death. Hence it is said: it is easy to set foot in a thorny thicket, but hard to turn around outside the night-luminous curtain; this is called clinging to the pole’s tip and sinking into dead water. Even that is not allowed to be dwelt in, how much less the state of one who has not yet reached insight, who has by chance won a flash-of-lightning samadhi and thinks he has attained it, juggling the shadows of the knowing spirit? This is the common disease of ancient and modern times in Chan practice: stopping short with a little gain. Fearing that such things would spread in the world and mislead many, when someone asked me for instruction I laughed and made the Song of the Board-Carrying Man to show him. The song says:

Board-carrying man, board-carrying man,
How have you let it cheat you so?
You think only of lightening your shoulder,
And never mind the rope that trips your heel.

Though you carry it back to before your birth,
Already it has hidden half of you.
This one board is a cangue on your neck;
All your flesh and bone belong to it.

If you do not throw it off at once,
It is your true enemy for a hundred thousand kalpas.
Walking, you are burdened; sitting, you are burdened.
The hindrance is plain — why do you not see?

Only because at the first you took it for real,
Has this pure house bred a demon.
Open your eyes and there it is; shut them and there it is;
Lightning flashes in the bright day’s void.

The phantom city’s image appears in the air,
And the foolish child takes it for a heavenly palace.
If you would be light, you must put it down.
A stinking dead toad is not worth the haggling.

Black beans traded for your eyes —
Fish eyes must be told from the real.
There is a road that is best to walk:
Level and broad as the scales of heaven.

Only do not linger among the flowers and willows,
And you will surely enter the imperial city in years to come.
Give up body and life as though they were the great earth;
Ox, horse, camel, donkey — you need not avoid them.

If you can truly cast it over Mount Sumeru,
Then the sword-tree and knife-mountain are a child’s play.
If you love it, it will harm you;
Its burden comes mostly of the care you spend on it.

One day smash the crystal bottle,
And the great earth’s mountains and rivers are all shattered.
I urge you, do not carry it.
The skull’s ooze dries up on the spot.

Divide your body and scatter your shadow into a hundred thousand million,
And from now on never enter the gate of birth and death.
Hearing That Shen Langqu Has Shut Himself in Retreat in the City of Gusu, I Send Him This Song

Light on water, color of hills, shadow upon shadow,
Interwoven past all hindrance.
Sometimes he sits and enters the land of lotus flowers,
Where the ground is level as a palm and spread with gold sand.

In the pool of eight virtues the lotuses open;
One touch of the fragrant wind opens the mind to awakening.
His ten-foot room has not a single wall,
Its measure holding the dharma-realm in equal vastness.

The ocean-assemblies of the ten directions enter within it;
He sits in contemplation and need not wander.
Mount Kuang hangs ten thousand fathoms in the vast void,
And yet it is as though he lived in the same room as you.

Not going out, not coming in, no coming or going —
Let me ask you: how is your mind at such a moment?
Poems on Following the Army (with Introduction)

Because I spread the Dharma I met with calamity, and by grace was sent into exile at Leiyang. In the second month of spring in the bing-shen year I entered Wuyang, and on the tenth day of the third month I reached the garrison post. At that time the place was in the grip of famine and plague, and had been for three years. There had been no rain for a whole year; the dead lay along the roads; weapons filled the eye; pestilence broke out on every side; the dead and wounded covered the fields. The scenes of misery were beyond words. On the road I walked, and wherever I looked my heart was stirred. By chance I made a number of regulated verses in the five-character form. Long steeped in withered stillness, I had not touched brush and ink; my words are rustic and coarse, and hardly form a piece. Yet the circumstances and feelings are true to life, and I trust they are not idle words. For the moment I record the events of one time.

Fleeing into exile, I take leave of the golden land,
And reach the barren wilds at the ocean’s edge.
The clouds’ aspect flies as a red bird;
The star’s tail trails a crimson snake.

Long since I cast away my staff and the woods grew;
I wave my halberd and the sun is not yet down.
From the southern sky to the northern passes,
Everywhere there is the barbarian reed-pipe.
Sitting Alone

This floating world lies outside my body;
This toilsome life is a wayside inn.
Who can with a single eye
Sweep empty the ten directions?

The blue sea flies a cool moon;
Green woods scatter the dawn wind.
On a folding chair I sit sprawled at ease,
Unconstrained, my meaning without end.
Returning to the Camp Gate at Evening
Four Poems on Events in the Gengzi Year

In the business of living men gladly own their clumsiness;
Spears and shields seethe like a boiling pot.
Gold and pearls they delight to heap up;
But reeds and straw they dread to be taxed for.

Who can settle the affairs of state?
The mind of Heaven cannot be relied on.
When will the southern warmth be played,
To wash away this burning heat?
Passing the Three Gorges
Lodging at Qingxi Post Station, in a Dream I Got the Lines “Grass Insects Chirr on the Broken Bank, Sand Birds Roost on the Cold Sandbar”; Thereupon I Completed the Poem
